This initiative is scheduled for the next budget period. 6.1.8.3.1.2 Air-Conditioners with Connected Thermostats The project team has identified two types of connected thermostats ideal for enhancing demand flexibility in air- conditioners: API-based (application programming interface) and those using direct internet (TCP/IP) communication. To support this, a VOLTTRON agent has been developed to interface with any API-based thermostat (e.g., ecobee4), enabling control over the air-conditioner via the building's Wi-Fi network. Through the thermostat's Internet API, the agent can remotely adjust temperature set points and retrieve telemetry data, such as current set points and indoor temperature, which are then stored in a database. Additionally, the same VOLTTRON agent can directly control specific thermostats (e.g., Venstar Explorer T2000 2-stage heat/2-stage cool) that have built-in Wi-Fi support and a documented local REST API (Representational State Transfer Application Programming Interface) for both data retrieval and control. This capability allows for complete monitoring and operation of the thermostat on the local area network, eliminating the need for vendor- provided cloud services. This initiative was scheduled for the next budget period. 25 6.1.8.3.1.3 Lighting Integration of building-controlled DERs for lighting has not yet been implemented. This initiative was scheduled for the next budget period, when lighting loads would have been incorporated into the existing control framework. At that stage, lighting systems would be registered in the equipment database and managed through the same API routing architecture currently used for chargers, solar, and battery assets. 6.1.8.3.1.4 Batteries In Budget Period 2, project activities advanced the operational role of battery energy storage systems (BESS) in supporting grid services. At the USU Microgrid Facility, the BESS demonstrated peak shaving during periods of high EVSE load and responded to OpenADR signals for external dispatch, showing the ability to absorb excess solar generation. The team also worked with the BESS vendor for Soliel Lofts and Citizen’s West project sites to enable testing and discussion of additional grid services on these enrolled devices. USU Microgrid Facility Batteries Figure 7: Integrated BESS and EVSE Power Utilization The USU microgrid facility uses an EMS to primarily peak-shave loads for when an EVSE is connected. In the above graph there is an EVSE that plugs in to charge at 100kW with the facility limit set to 70kW. Ten minutes into the first charge a second EVSE connected into a second charger and charged at 100kW as well for a total draw of 200kW while the EMS system dispatched the energy to maintain a load of about 75kW from the grid. After the EVSEs finished charging the battery that was used to shave the peak was charged at a rate that kept the utility power at 65kW until fully charged. 26 To accomplish balancing load at the USU microgrid a SEL device is used for sampling at a 30Hz rate.
